reasoning_traces.think: This chapter introduces a novel user authentication framework leveraging pressure sensor arrays embedded within a helmet. The system operates under the premise that individual gripping behaviors are unique and can be captured through pressure variations across multiple sensor locations. The core methodology involves acquiring pressure data from 32 sensors distributed across the helmet’s interior—top, sides, back, and cheek pads—and computing a 32-dimensional feature vector representing the average pressure over a defined time window. These features are then fed into an SVM classifier trained on pre-registered user data. Authentication proceeds only when the cumulative pressure exceeds a predefined threshold (159 V), ensuring that the helmet is being worn correctly. Experimental validation shows high accuracy in distinguishing trained users from untrained ones, with mean acceptance rates of 85.4% and rejection rates of 82.65%. The approach builds upon prior work in biometric authentication using pressure sensors, extending it to helmet-based wearable systems. It emphasizes robustness against spoofing attempts by relying on behavioral traits rather than static identifiers. The design supports real-time operation and integrates seamlessly with existing helmet infrastructure, making it suitable for applications in safety-critical environments such as cycling or aviation.
